etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hey, from Old English hīeġ, from Proto-West Germanic *hawi, from Proto-Germanic *hawją (compare West Frisian hea, Dutch hooi, German Heu, Norwegian høy), from *hawwaną (“to hew, cut down”). More at hew.

definitions.definition: (uncountable) Grass cut and dried for use as animal fodder.

quote.citation: 1605, M. N. [pseudonym; William Camden], Remaines of a Greater Worke, Concerning Britaine, […], London:  […]  G[eorge] E[ld] for Simon Waterson, →OCLC:
1857, Charles Louis Flint, Grasses and Forage Plants: A Practical Treatise,  […] :
quote.text: Hay may be dried too much as well as too little.

definitions.definition: (countable) Any mix of green leafy plants used for fodder.

quote.text: I would like some of that hay. Enclose $20.

quote.citation: 1994, “Bug Powder Dust”, performed by Bomb the Bass:
quote.text: Jeff Spicoli, roll me another hay

definitions.definition: A net set around the haunt of an animal, especially a rabbit.
To cut grasses or herb plants for use as animal fodder.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English haye, heye, a conflation of Old English heġe (“hedge, fence”) and Old English ġehæġ (“an enclosed piece of land”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A net placed around the lair or burrow of an animal.

quote.citation: 1594, Christopher Marlow[e], The Troublesome Raigne and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second, King of England: […], London:  […]  [Eliot’s Court Press] for Henry Bell, […], published 1622, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: My men like Satyres grazing on the lawnes,Shall with their Goate feete daunce an antick hay,

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “Loues Labour’s Lost”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: I’ll make one in a dance, or so; or I will playOn the tabour to the Worthies, and let them dance the hay.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From the sound it represents, by analogy with other letters such as kay and gay. The expected form in English if the h had survived in the Latin name of the letter "h", hā.

definitions.definition: The letter for the h sound in Pitman shorthand.
